title: Yard Dog Landscapes Blog
description: Practical lawn care, landscaping, and yard advice from the crew at Yard Dog Landscapes, written for East Texas homeowners.

items.title: Best Months to Prune Trees in East Texas
items.summary: Late winter before bud break is the pruning window for most East Texas trees. What to cut now, what to wait on, and why topping is never the answer.

items.title: When to Book Christmas Lights in East Texas
items.summary: Christmas light installs in East Texas run through Thanksgiving week and the calendar fills. How a professional install works and what to decide before you call.

items.title: What to Cut Back in Fall in East Texas Beds (and What to Leave)
items.summary: Which perennials to cut back after the first frost in East Texas and which to leave standing until late winter, why seed heads and hollow stems are worth keeping, and a simple bed cleanup order that ends with fresh mulch.

items.title: First Freeze Prep in East Texas: What to Do and What to Skip
items.summary: The first freeze in Gregg County usually lands in mid-November. What is worth covering, why a deep watering beats a bedsheet, how to protect exposed irrigation plumbing, and the pruning to leave alone until late winter.

items.title: When to Stop Fertilizing Your East Texas Lawn
items.summary: Why fertilizer in November is wasted on a bermuda or St. Augustine lawn in East Texas, what late nitrogen does to tender growth before a freeze, how a soil test tells you what spring needs, and what to do for the lawn right now instead.

items.title: Ryegrass Overseeding in East Texas: Usually Not Worth It
items.summary: Why mid-October is the only window that works for ryegrass in East Texas, the winter mowing and watering it commits you to, why it can slow bermuda green-up in spring, and why St. Augustine should never be overseeded.

items.title: Planting Winter Color in East Texas in November
items.summary: October is the ideal window for pansies and violas in East Texas, but early November still works. Which cool-season annuals hold up through a Longview winter, why bed drainage matters in our clay, and the light feeding that keeps them blooming.

items.title: Mulch the First Leaves, Rake the Last Ones
items.summary: The first light leaf fall in early October can go straight back into an East Texas lawn through the mower deck. Where the line is, why post oak, sweetgum, and pecan litter starts smothering St. Augustine, and the week in November when mulching stops working.

items.title: The Fall Window That Decides How Many Winter Weeds You Fight in February
items.summary: Fall pre-emergent in East Texas is timed off soil temperature falling through 70 degrees, not off a date on the calendar. Why that window sets how much annual bluegrass, henbit, and chickweed you fight in February, and why watering it in is not optional.

items.title: Beds Need a Fall Top-Dress, Not a Full Mulch Reload
items.summary: Why a thin fall top-dress beats stripping and reloading a bed in September, how much of last spring's mulch has already turned into soil, what a winter mulch layer does for roots in East Texas clay, and why mulch piled against stems causes more damage than no mulch at all.

items.title: Fall Beats Spring for Planting Trees and Shrubs in East Texas
items.summary: September through November is the real planting window in East Texas. Why warm soil under cooling air lets a new tree build roots for six months before it ever sees heat, how to water a new tree through a Longview winter, and why a spring-planted tree spends its first summer in survival mode instead of growing.

items.title: The Webbed Nests Taking Over East Texas Pecans in Late Summer
items.summary: Those white webs swallowing the ends of pecan and sweetgum branches in September are fall webworms, not bagworms and not tent caterpillars. How to tell the three apart, why our trees get hit hardest, when pruning a nest out is worth the trouble, and when a mature tree just shrugs it off before leaf drop.

items.title: Late August Is When You Set Up Your Fall Lawn, Not September
items.summary: The East Texas fall lawn reset gets decided in the last two weeks of August, not in September. When to aerate warm-season turf, why the last real nitrogen feeding goes down earlier than the bag suggests, and whether overseeding is worth it on bermuda and St. Augustine.

items.title: The Late-Summer Grub Damage That Peels Up Like Carpet
items.summary: Turf that lifts like a rug with no roots underneath isn't drought stress, it's white grubs. The ten-second tug test, the birds and armadillos tell, and why late August is when East Texas grub damage gets ugly fast.

items.title: Stop Topping Your Crepe Myrtles: The Case Against Crape Murder
items.summary: Topping a crepe myrtle back to knuckled stubs doesn't make it bloom more. It makes it grow back taller on weaker wood. How to spot a topped tree in August, how to prune one correctly in February, and how to bring a butchered crepe myrtle back.

items.title: Armyworms Can Strip an East Texas Lawn Overnight in Late Summer
items.summary: A green bermuda lawn can go tan in a day when fall armyworms march through. Here's how to read the frosted-tip and bird-flocking warning signs, the soapy-water test that confirms it in five minutes, and why worm size decides whether the lawn recovers.

items.title: Why St. Augustine Dies in the Sunniest Part of the Yard in Late Summer
items.summary: A dead patch in the sunniest part of a St. Augustine lawn in late summer usually isn't drought. It's chinch bugs. Here's how to scout the green-to-brown edge, why the hottest yards get hit first, and why watering it more makes it worse.

items.title: When Your East Texas Yard Needs a French Drain (And When It Doesn't)
items.summary: Standing water after every rain doesn't always mean you need a French drain. Here's how to trace where the water is really coming from, the cheaper grading and downspout fixes that solve most soggy yards, and what a real drain install actually costs in East Texas.

items.title: Why Mowing Shorter in Summer Backfires
items.summary: Cutting your lawn short to skip a mow is the fastest way to cook it in an East Texas July. Short grass grows short roots and opens the door to crabgrass. Here are the right July deck heights for bermuda and St. Augustine.

items.title: The Five Plants That Actually Survive a Longview July
items.summary: Most bedding plants look great in May and cook by mid-July. These five, lantana, vinca, salvia, plumbago, and knockout roses, take a Longview summer and hold their color into fall. Here's how we plant each one.

items.title: Brown Patch vs. Heat Stress: How to Tell the Difference (Before You Make It Worse)
items.summary: Two East Texas lawns can go brown the same week for opposite reasons, and the fix for one kills the other. Here's how to tell fungus rings from heat stress before you grab the hose and make it worse.

items.title: What You Should and Shouldn't Prune in June
items.summary: In East Texas, a June haircut helps some plants and kills the bloom on others. Here's the difference between crepe myrtles, hollies, hydrangeas, and azaleas, plus the one tree you should never cut this time of year.

items.title: Why We Don't Put Landscape Fabric Under Mulch
items.summary: Landscape fabric under mulch sounds like a permanent fix for weeds. In two or three years it's usually the worst weed bed on the block, and a mess to tear out. Here's what actually happens and what we do instead.

items.title: The Three Irrigation Mistakes That Cook East Texas Lawns
items.summary: Your sprinklers run every day and the lawn still looks cooked by July. It's usually one of three mistakes: wrong time, wrong schedule, or a broken head nobody's noticed. Here's how to audit your own system in 20 minutes.

items.title: Why Fire Ants Explode in May (and What Actually Kills the Mound)
items.summary: Fire ant mounds pop up everywhere in May for a reason. Most people treat them the slow, expensive way. Here's the two-product system that actually works in East Texas, and the order matters.

items.title: Bermuda vs. St. Augustine in East Texas: Which Grass Fits Your Yard
items.summary: Bermuda loves sun and foot traffic. St. Augustine handles shade. In East Texas, picking wrong means a thin, struggling lawn no fertilizer can fix. Here's how we decide on every property.

items.title: How Much Mulch You Actually Need in East Texas (It's Less Than You Think)
items.summary: Big-box stores tell you 3 inches of mulch. We do 1 to 1.5 inches and the beds look better, the weeds stay down, and your plants don't suffocate. Here's the math and the reason.

items.title: The East Texas Fertilization Window Most Homeowners Miss
items.summary: Most people fertilize too early or too late. The May window in East Texas is short, real, and most homeowners blow right through it. Here's what to put down, when, and what we see go wrong.

items.title: Why Your East Texas Lawn Looks Worse in July (And What Actually Helps)
items.summary: Mid-July yard looking rough? Most East Texas lawn problems come from a handful of fixable mistakes. Here's what we see on almost every property, and what to change before this summer cooks your grass again.
